Eigenvalues describe long-time modes of a linear system, while singular values describe its largest Euclidean amplification at a given time.
Here $h(t)$ is a finite-dimensional [state vector]{.term key="state-vector"} and $A$ is a constant square matrix representing a linear map in a chosen coordinate system.
The central question is whether a disturbance decays, grows temporarily, or grows without bound; these are different questions about the same dynamics.
The related matrix properties and inverse identities explain how these systems can be analysed and computed.

## Matrix properties {#properties}

Write $A^*$ for conjugate transpose and $A^\top$ for ordinary transpose.

| Property | Definition or characterisation |
|---|---|
| Real symmetric | $A^\top=A$. |
| Complex Hermitian | $A^*=A$. |
| Normal | $A^*A=AA^*$. |
| Orthogonal | Real square $Q$ with $Q^\top Q=I$. |
| Unitary | Complex square $U$ with $U^*U=I$. |
| Diagonalisable | $A=V\Lambda V^{-1}$ for an invertible eigenvector matrix $V$. |

A real matrix is orthogonally diagonalisable exactly when it is symmetric.
A complex matrix is unitarily diagonalisable exactly when it is normal.
General diagonalisation does not imply that the eigenvectors are orthogonal.
For compatible dimensions, singular values are the nonnegative square roots of the eigenvalues of $A^*A$.
The spectral norm $\|A\|_2$ is its largest singular value.

## Modes and long-time stability {#modes}

Consider the autonomous continuous-time system $\dot h=Ah$, with no external forcing.
Its solution is $h(t)=e^{tA}h(0)$.
If $A=V\Lambda V^{-1}$, then

$$
  e^{tA}=V\operatorname{diag}(e^{t\lambda_i})V^{-1}.
$$

The real part of each eigenvalue controls exponential growth or decay; its imaginary part controls oscillation.
Asymptotic stability here means every initial state tends to zero as time tends to infinity.
All eigenvalues having strictly negative real parts implies asymptotic stability in finite dimensions.
Purely imaginary eigenvalues require more care: a nontrivial Jordan block can introduce polynomial growth even when exponential growth rates are zero.
Calling a matrix “coupled” also depends on coordinates; a diagonalisable system has independent modal equations in its eigenvector basis.

## Transient amplification {#transient-amplification}

For a fixed time, the largest possible amplification in the [Euclidean norm]{.term key="euclidean-norm"} over nonzero initial states is

$$
  G(t)=\sup_{h_0\ne0}\frac{\|e^{tA}h_0\|_2}{\|h_0\|_2}
  =\|e^{tA}\|_2.
$$

Define $G_{\max}=\sup_{t\geq0}G(t)$.
An asymptotically stable non-normal matrix can have $G_{\max}>1$, but non-normality alone does not force it.
For a normal matrix, $G(t)=\max_i e^{t\operatorname{Re}\lambda_i}$, so strictly negative real parts give monotone decay.

For a concrete comparison, take

$$
  A_\kappa=\begin{pmatrix}-1&\kappa\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Both $\kappa=1$ and $\kappa=4$ give eigenvalues $-1,-1$ and eventual decay.
The first never increases any state's Euclidean norm, while the second initially amplifies some states.
Eigenvalues alone therefore do not determine the largest transient amplification.
The conclusion concerns the specified norm and coordinate representation; changing either can change the amplification being measured.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Proof and counterexample: non-normal does not mean transient growth"}

For real dynamics,

$$
  \frac{d}{dt}\|h\|_2^2=h^\top(A+A^\top)h.
$$

If $A+A^\top$ is negative semidefinite, the norm cannot increase for any initial state.
Consider

$$
  A=\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

This matrix is non-normal, but the eigenvalues of $A+A^\top$ are $-1$ and $-3$.
Every nonzero state therefore has decreasing squared norm, despite non-normality.
In contrast, replacing the upper-right entry by $4$ gives $A+A^\top$ eigenvalues $2$ and $-6$.
An initial vector in the positive eigendirection has initial norm growth, even though both eigenvalues of $A$ remain $-1$.
Both systems eventually decay; only the second has transient amplification above its initial norm for some input state.

:::

## Woodbury and low-rank corrections {#woodbury}

Low-rank matrix structure can reduce the size of an inverse calculation.
The reduction is useful when the base inverse can already be applied efficiently.
Let $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ and $C\in\mathbb C^{r\times r}$ be invertible, with $U\in\mathbb C^{n\times r}$ and $V\in\mathbb C^{r\times n}$.
Assume the remaining inverse below exists, and define

$$
  S=C^{-1}+VA^{-1}U.
$$

The Woodbury identity is

$$
  (A+UCV)^{-1}
  =A^{-1}-A^{-1}US^{-1}VA^{-1}.
$$

The correction has a minus sign.
For $r\ll n$, the additional inverse is only $r\times r$.
S4 uses related structured inverses in its kernel calculation; see [S4, Appendix C](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.00396).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: checking the sign in Woodbury"}

Let $R=A^{-1}-A^{-1}US^{-1}VA^{-1}$.
Since $CS=I+CVA^{-1}U$,

$$
  (A+UCV)A^{-1}U=UCS.
$$

Multiplying out gives

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  (A+UCV)R
  &=I+UCVA^{-1}\\
  &\quad-UCS S^{-1}VA^{-1}\\
  &=I.
  \end{aligned}
$$

Thus $R$ is the inverse under the stated assumptions.
The scalar check $A=C=U=V=1$ gives $(1+1)^{-1}=1-1/2$, immediately detecting the incorrect plus sign.

:::
